name: INA280A1IDCKR
title: 2.7-V to 120-V, 1.1-MHz high-side current-sense amplifier, SC-70
summary: INA280 is a high-side, unidirectional current-sense amplifier whose inputs work from 2.7 V to 120 V common mode while the part runs from a 2.7-V to 20-V supply. Five fixed gains from 20 V/V to 500 V/V are offered, with offset within ±150 µV, gain error within ±0.5% and a typical DC CMRR of 140 dB. Bandwidth reaches 1.1 MHz at gain 20 with a 2 V/µs slew rate, for fast overcurrent detection. It comes in a 5-pin SC-70 package.

circuits.title: Typical application, high-side sensing into an ADC
circuits.description: The shunt RSENSE carries the load current from the bus VCM down to the load, which returns to ground. IN+ connects at the bus end of the shunt and IN– at the load end. OUT drives the input of a SAR ADC whose ground is shared with GND. The amplifier is powered from its own VS supply.

circuits.title: Unidirectional sensing on a 48-V supply
circuits.description: Current flows from a 48-V supply through RSENSE into the load. IN+ sits on the supply side of the shunt and IN– on the load side, so only current flowing toward the load is measured. The amplifier runs from 5 V and OUT gives the scaled shunt voltage.

circuits.title: Differential filter at the input pins
circuits.description: Each end of the shunt reaches its input pin through a series resistor RIN, and CIN joins IN+ to IN– after the two resistors, forming a differential low-pass with f3dB = 1 / (4π RIN CIN). RIN is kept at 10 Ω or less, because the input bias currents flowing in RIN add a gain error.
notes: The part measures accurately without an input filter, and a filter at the inputs is not recommended.

circuits.title: Drain current of an RF power amplifier
circuits.description: A 54-V rail feeds an RF power transistor through the shunt and a drain choke. The junction of shunt and choke also connects through a capacitor and an RF element to RF Out. The INA280A2 (50 V/V) senses across the shunt; its output passes through a series resistor to a capacitor to ground and into an ADC read by a microprocessor. The microprocessor drives the transistor's gate through an RF DAC and a coupling capacitor. With a 5-A maximum and a 5-V supply, the shunt is 15 mΩ.
notes: The INA280 supply of 5 V is the example's design value.

operation.text: INA280 is a single current-sense amplifier in a 5-pin SC-70 (DCK) package with five fixed gains, A1 to A5 in turn: 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500 V/V. It runs from 2.7 V to 20 V, draws 370 µA typical and is specified from −40 °C to +125 °C. An automotive version, INA280-Q1, exists.

A transconductance input stage built round a current-feedback amplifier converts the shunt voltage, across matched input resistors R1, into a current that flows in an internal load resistor RL to ground; a buffer drives OUT from that node. This lets the inputs sit up to 120 V common mode with about 20 µA of bias current per input.

The inputs work from 2.7 V to 120 V common mode and survive −20 V to +122 V. The lowest usable common-mode voltage rises with the supply (2.7 V at low supplies, near 7 V at VS = 20 V). The input structure only allows high-side sensing.
The −3-dB bandwidth falls with gain, from 1.1 MHz at 20 V/V to 800 kHz at 500 V/V, and also falls as VSENSE, and so the output voltage, gets smaller.

Gain comes from an internal resistor network whose ratios match closely but whose absolute values spread widely, so adding outside resistance to change the gain is not recommended. Gain error is within 0.5% for every option, with drift up to 20 ppm/°C over −40 °C to +125 °C.
The output can swing up to VS. With gain 20 V/V the largest usable differential input is 1 V. The inputs may sit well above the supply: VS up to 20 V while IN+ and IN– go to 120 V.
Only current flowing from the supply to the load is measured. At zero current the output can sit up to 25 mV above GND, so a sense voltage of at least 25 mV / Gain keeps the output linear.
With 1.1 MHz bandwidth and 2 V/µs slew rate, with a 2-mΩ shunt, gain 20 and a 75-A trip level, the output reaches 3 V in under 2 µs.
A negative differential input overloads the amplifier; once VSENSE turns positive again it needs time to recover, and the more negative VSENSE was, the longer that takes.

A larger shunt improves accuracy because offset matters less, but power dissipation and the output swing limits cap it: IMAX × RSENSE × GAIN must stay below the positive swing, and IMIN × RSENSE × GAIN above the negative swing. A higher gain allows a smaller shunt with less dissipation; for 10 A full scale and a 5-V output, the shunt runs from 25 mΩ (2.5 W) at A1 down to 1 mΩ (0.1 W) at A5.

No input filter is needed. A filter at the output raises the output impedance seen by the next stage. A filter at the inputs uses series resistors of 10 Ω or less: the bias currents differ when a differential voltage is present, so a drop in the resistors, and their mismatch, adds error. Internal bias resistance RB is 6600 Ω ± 20%.

The supply can be up to 20 V while the load rail at IN+ and IN– goes to 120 V. The output range is set by VS and the swing-to-supply limit. The bypass capacitor is 0.1 µF, placed as close to VS and GND as possible; more capacitance helps with a noisy or high-impedance supply.

Run the inputs to the shunt as a Kelvin (4-wire) connection so only the shunt's resistance lies between them, and keep those traces short. In a recommended layout the bypass capacitor sits beside VS (pin 3) with a via to the ground plane, the shunt sits across IN+ (pin 4) and IN– (pin 5) with the bus on the IN+ side and the load on the IN– side, and OUT (pin 1) leaves on the opposite side.
